# Fallibilism (all knowledge of nature is provisional) (`fallibilism_provisional_knowledge`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/ideas.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Scientific method & philosophical ideas (`ideas`)
- Deps: helped by scientific_method, bayesian_reasoning
- Core idea: Nothing about the natural world is known with final certainty; every claim is held with a degree of confidence that should follow the evidence and be revised when the evidence changes. This does not mean all opinions are equally good: some claims have survived so many attempts to refute them that doubting them is unreasonable, and later theories usually keep earlier ones as close approximations (a flat earth is nearly right for a field, a sphere for a voyage, a slightly flattened sphere for a geodesist). In practice: say how sure you are and why, state what would change your mind, and treat your own remembered schoolbook facts in the same way. For a time traveller this is also honesty, since half-remembered knowledge is exactly where confident errors hide.
- Pitfalls:
  - Saying 'science has proved' or 'we now know for certain'
  - Sliding into relativism: 'everything is just a theory, so my guess is as good as yours'
  - Describing superseded theories as simply wrong; Ptolemy predicts planets well and Newton still builds bridges
  - Preaching universal doubt in a religious setting, where it is heard as doubt of revelation; limit the claim to knowledge of nature gained by the senses
  - Never committing: a patron needs a recommendation with honest odds, not a list of doubts
- History: greece: c. 500 BC – Xenophanes: no man knows the clear truth, but by seeking we find better; 2nd c. BC Carneades' degrees of plausibility; c. 200 AD Sextus Empiricus; india: c. 500 BC onwards – Jain doctrine of conditional assertion (syadvada); c. 200 AD Nagarjuna; c. 800 the sceptic Jayarasi; china: c. 300 BC – Zhuangzi on the limits of every standpoint; islamic: early 11th c. – in Doubts about Ptolemy Ibn al-Haytham urges the critic to question his own judgement; c. 1108 al-Ghazali, Deliverance from Error, examines the grounds of certainty; europe: 1562 – Sextus printed in Latin; 1580 Montaigne; 1739–1748 Hume's problem of induction; c. 1897 Peirce coins 'fallibilism'; 1934 Popper
- Read:
  - Sextus Empiricus, Outlines of Pyrrhonism (c. 200)
  - Richard H. Popkin, The History of Scepticism: From Savonarola to Bayle (2003)
  - Isaac Asimov, The Relativity of Wrong (1988)
